lessons.title: Describe the Data Using the Median
lessons.objective: I can find the median of a data set and use it to describe what is typical.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain the median using the words order, middle, typical, and half.

concept.heading: What are mean, median, and mode?
concept.intro: Mean, median, and mode are three ways to find the center, or "typical" value, of a data set. The mean is the average, the median is the middle, and the mode is the most common value.
concept.keyIdea: Measures of Center: Median. Formula: Median = Middle value in an ordered set. 1. Order all data values from least to greatest. 2. Odd count: The median is the exact center number. 3. Even count: The median is the mean of the two middle numbers

worked.title: Watch me find the median
lines: My data set: 2, 4, 4, 6, 9 — five values, already in order. Ordering first is what makes a middle exist at all.
With 5 values, the middle is the 3rd one. Counting in from both ends: 2 and 9 pair off, 4 and 6 pair off, and 4 is left alone.
So the median is 4. Half the values sit at or below it and half at or above it.
Now an even set: 2, 4, 6, 9. There is no single middle, so I take the mean of the two middle values: (4 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5. The median is 5, even though 5 is not in the data.
linesEs: Mi conjunto de datos: 2, 4, 4, 6, 9 — cinco valores, ya ordenados. Ordenar primero es lo que hace que exista un medio.
Con 5 valores, el del medio es el 3.º. Contando desde ambos extremos: 2 y 9 se emparejan, 4 y 6 se emparejan, y el 4 queda solo.
Entonces la mediana es 4. La mitad de los valores queda en él o por debajo, y la mitad en él o por encima.
Ahora un conjunto par: 2, 4, 6, 9. No hay un solo valor del medio, así que tomo la media de los dos centrales: (4 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5. La mediana es 5, aunque el 5 no esté en los datos.

together.title: Let's do one together
lines: New data set, out of order: 13, 3, 7, 10, 7. Put it in order first.
In order: 3, 7, 7, 10, 13. Five values, so the middle is the 3rd.
The median is 7. Say what it means: a typical value in this set is about 7.
Now change the 13 to 130. Does the median move? It does not — still 7. That resistance is exactly why the median is used.
linesEs: Conjunto de datos nuevo, desordenado: 13, 3, 7, 10, 7. Ordénalo primero.
En orden: 3, 7, 7, 10, 13. Cinco valores, así que el del medio es el 3.º.
La mediana es 7. Di lo que significa: un valor típico de este conjunto es aproximadamente 7.
Ahora cambia el 13 por 130. ¿Se mueve la mediana? No se mueve — sigue siendo 7. Esa resistencia es exactamente por lo que se usa la mediana.

vocabulary.term: Describe the Data Using the Median
vocabulary.definition: Using the middle value of the ordered data to say what is typical for the whole set.
The middle number when you put them in order.
vocabulary.example: Data: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 → the middle (3rd) value is 5, so median = 5

vocabulary.definition: The number that shows up most often.
vocabulary.example: Data: 2, 3, 3, 5, 7 → 3 appears twice (most often), so mode = 3

vocabulary.definition: A number that is much bigger or smaller than the rest.
vocabulary.example: Data: 10, 12, 11, 13, 50 → 50 is far from the others, so 50 is an outlier

vocabulary.definition: How the data looks: where it sits and how spread out it is.
vocabulary.example: If most values cluster in the center with fewer at the ends, the distribution is symmetric

vocabulary.definition: How spread out the numbers are.
vocabulary.example: 8, 9, 10, 11 has low variability (close together); 2, 10, 25, 40 has high variability (far apart)

vocabulary.definition: One number that describes a typical value in a data set.
vocabulary.example: The median is one measure of center.

vocabulary.definition: The number exactly between the two middle values of an even-count data set.
vocabulary.example: Between 18 and 22, the halfway value is 20.

lessons.title: Represent and Describe Data in a Box Plot
lessons.objective: I can make and read a box plot to summarize a data set.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my box plot using the words box plot, median, quartile, and interquartile range.

concept.heading: What is a box plot?
concept.intro: A box plot is a simple picture that shows how a set of data is spread out, using just five key numbers: the lowest value, the first quartile (Q1), the median (middle), the third quartile (Q3), and the highest value.
concept.keyIdea: Box Plots & 5-Number Summary. Formula: IQR = Q3 − Q1. 1. 5-Number Summary: Minimum, Lower Quartile (Q1), Median (Q2), Upper Quartile (Q3), Maximum. 2. Draw the Box: The box spans from Q1 to Q3 and contains the middle 50% of data. 3. Whiskers: Draw lines from the box out to the minimum and maximum

worked.title: Watch me build one
lines: My data, in order: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 18, 22, 24, 28. There are 11 numbers.
The middle number is the 6th one, 14, so the median = 14.
The lower half is 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Its middle is 8, so Q1 = 8.
The upper half is 15, 18, 22, 24, 28. Its middle is 22, so Q3 = 22.
The lowest is 4 and the highest is 28. I draw a box from 8 to 22, a line at 14, and whiskers out to 4 and 28.
linesEs: Mis datos, en orden: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 18, 22, 24, 28. Hay 11 números.
El número del medio es el 6.º, que es 14, así que la mediana = 14.
La mitad inferior es 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Su valor del medio es 8, así que Q1 = 8.
La mitad superior es 15, 18, 22, 24, 28. Su valor del medio es 22, así que Q3 = 22.
El menor es 4 y el mayor es 28. Dibujo una caja de 8 a 22, una línea en 14 y bigotes hasta 4 y 28.

together.title: Let's try one together
lines: New, smaller data set: 2, 5, 5, 8, 11. First, what is the median (the middle value)?
The lower half is 2, 5 and the upper half is 8, 11. What is Q1? What is Q3?
What are the lowest and highest values? Now picture the box stretching from Q1 to Q3 with the median line inside.
linesEs: Conjunto de datos nuevo y más pequeño: 2, 5, 5, 8, 11. Primero, ¿cuál es la mediana (el valor del medio)?
La mitad inferior es 2, 5 y la mitad superior es 8, 11. ¿Cuánto es Q1? ¿Cuánto es Q3?
¿Cuáles son el valor menor y el mayor? Ahora imagina la caja extendiéndose de Q1 a Q3 con la línea de la mediana adentro.

vocabulary.definition: Show a data set's five-number summary in a box-and-whisker display.
vocabulary.example: minimum | Q1 [ median ] Q3 | maximum

vocabulary.definition: A graph that shows how data is spread using five key numbers.
vocabulary.example: A box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, and whiskers from min to max

vocabulary.definition: The middle number when you put them in order.
vocabulary.example: Data: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 → median is 20 (the 3rd value)

vocabulary.definition: Numbers that split the data into four equal parts.
vocabulary.example: Data: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 → Q1 = 4 (median of lower half), Q3 = 12 (median of upper half)

vocabulary.definition: The spread of the middle half of the data (Q3 − Q1).
vocabulary.example: If Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 20, then IQR = 20 − 12 = 8 — the middle 50% spans 8 units

vocabulary.definition: How the data looks: where it sits and how spread out it is.
vocabulary.example: A box plot where the median is centered in the box shows symmetric distribution

vocabulary.definition: How spread out the numbers are.
vocabulary.example: Small IQR = low variability in the middle 50%. Large IQR = high variability

vocabulary.definition: The minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum of a data set.
vocabulary.example: 6, 8, 14, 19, 22 — the five values a box plot is built from.

vocabulary.definition: A line on a box plot that reaches from the box out to the least or greatest value.
vocabulary.example: The left whisker reaches the minimum; the right whisker reaches the maximum.

vocabulary.definition: The values from the first quartile to the third quartile, which the box covers.
vocabulary.example: The box holds half of the data.

feedback: Did you forget to divide by the count of numbers?
Add the numbers first—does 14 equal the sum divided by 5?
Is 60 the mean, or the sum?
hints: Mean means the average of all five numbers — you'll need both a total and how many numbers there are.
Use the formula: mean = sum of the values ÷ how many values. Count first: there are 5 numbers here.
Step 1: add 10 + 14 + 8 + 12 + 16 to get the total. Then divide that total by 5 — the result is the mean.

feedback: The lowest value is 3, but the median is the MIDDLE value, not the smallest. Put them in order first: 2, 3, 5, 7, 9.
5.2 is the MEAN — you added all five values and divided by 5. The median asks for the middle value after ordering, which is a different measure.
7 is in the list, but it is not in the middle once the values are ordered: 2, 3, 5, 7, 9. Count in from both ends.
hints: Median = the middle number, but only AFTER the list is in order. Don't pick the middle of the unsorted list.
Rewrite 3, 7, 2, 9, 5 from least to greatest, then count in from both ends until you reach the one value in the exact middle.
Start ordering: the smallest is 2, then 3... finish the ordered list of all five values, then circle the 3rd one — that's the median.

support.explanation: 4 appears three times — more than any other value. Mode = 4.
feedback: 2 appears once—is mode the smallest or most frequent?
7 appears once—which number appears most often?
9 appears once—count how many times each number shows up.
hints: Mode is about repeats — which value shows up in the list more times than any other?
Make a quick tally: write each different number and count how many times it appears in 4, 7, 4, 9, 2, 4, 8.
Start your tally: 7 appears once, 9 appears once... keep counting every number and pick the one with the highest tally.

feedback: Add them up first, then divide by 5—not just multiply.
Count the numbers (5)—divide the sum by 5.
This is the sum—is sum the same as mean?
hints: Watch out: one tempting answer is just the total of the list. The mean asks you to go one step further.
Mean = total ÷ count. There are 5 values in this list, so after adding you must divide by 5.
Step 1: add 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 + 14. Step 2: take that total and divide it by 5. The quotient is your mean.

steps: Data set: A player scored 6, 8, 10, and 6 points in 4 games.
Goal: Find the MEAN number of points.
support.explanation: Adding is only half of the mean. After adding (sum = 30) you must DIVIDE by how many values there are: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5. The mean is 7.5 points, not 30.
hints: Mean = add then DIVIDE. The total of 30 is just the sum, not the mean.
There are 4 values, so divide the sum by 4: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5.

support.prompt: A box plot shows: Min = 10, Q1 = 15, Median = 20, Q3 = 28, Max = 35. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
feedback: Full range from min to max is 25, but IQR is different.
IQR only uses the quartiles, not min and max.
This is the spread, but IQR is Q3 − Q1 only.
hints: You're given five numbers, but IQR only uses two of them: Q1 and Q3. Ignore the min, median, and max.
IQR = Q3 − Q1. Find Q3 (28) and Q1 (15) in the summary — the IQR is their difference, the width of the box.
Set up the subtraction Q3 − Q1: that's 28 − 15. The difference you get is the IQR.

support.prompt: On a box plot, what does the line inside the box represent?
support.explanation: The line inside the box of a box plot always represents the median.
feedback: The line shows center—but mean is a different measure.
The line is always the middle value, not an average.
The range is a spread — the whole distance from the smallest value to the largest — not a single line drawn inside the box. Think about which value splits the data in half.
hints: Picture a box plot: a box with whiskers, and a line cutting through the box. That line marks the CENTER of the data.
The box runs from Q1 to Q3, so the line inside splits the middle 50% in half. Think about which measure splits ordered data into halves.
First step: recall which measure means 'the middle value of the ordered data.' The line inside the box always marks that exact measure.

support.prompt: What percentage of data falls between Q1 and Q3 on a box plot?
support.explanation: The box in a box plot contains the middle 50% of the data (from Q1 to Q3).
feedback: The box shows the inner half—is it 25%?
Q1 to Q3 is the middle section—what fraction is that?
Each quarter is 25%—Q1 to Q3 is two quarters.
hints: Quartiles cut the data into 4 equal parts — 'quart' like 'quarter.' Each part holds the same share of the data.
Each quarter of the data is 25%. Count how many quarters sit between Q1 and Q3: Q1 to the median, then the median to Q3.
First step: Q1 to the median is one quarter — 25%. Add the quarter from the median up to Q3 to get the box's total share.

feedback: Max is 31, min is 8—range is the difference.
Range is spread—subtract max from min, don't add.
Find max and min—is range the minimum?
hints: Range = how far the data stretches: the gap between the biggest and smallest values only. The middle values don't matter.
Scan the list 14, 22, 8, 31, 17: find the maximum and the minimum, then subtract the min from the max.
First step: the max is 31 and the min is 8. Set up 31 − 8 — that difference is the range.

steps: Box plot values: Bobcats' box plot: Min = 10, Q1 = 18, Median = 24, Q3 = 30, Max = 40
support.explanation: The IQR is Q3 MINUS Q1, not Q3 plus Q1. IQR = 30 − 18 = 12. The student added the quartiles instead of subtracting, so 48 is much larger than the actual spread of the middle 50%, which is only 12 points.
hints: IQR stands for InterQuartile RANGE — a range is found by subtracting, not adding.

core.prompt: Data set: 4, 6, 6, 8, 10, 12. What is the median?
core.explanation: With 6 values, the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values: (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.
feedback: With an even count, take the average of the two middle values.
Don't add all values and divide—find the middle two values.
The two middle values are 6 and 8—what's their average?
hints: Count the values: there are 6, an even number — so no single value sits exactly in the middle.
With an even count, the median is the average of the TWO middle values. In an ordered list of 6, those are the 3rd and 4th.
The list is already ordered. Step 1: circle the 3rd and 4th values. Step 2: add them and divide by 2 — that result is the median.

steps: Data set: Points per game, in order: 3, 8, 10, 14, 16, 20 (6 values)
Goal: Find the MEDIAN number of points.
Pick the middle: With 6 values the student grabs a single middle number and says median = 10.
core.explanation: When a data set has an EVEN number of values there is no single middle number. You must average the TWO middle values. Here the 3rd and 4th values are 10 and 14, so the median = (10 + 14) ÷ 2 = 12, not 10.
hints: With an even number of values, there are two numbers in the middle — average them.
The two middle values are 10 and 14: (10 + 14) ÷ 2 = 12.

core.prompt: Two box plots show: Team A has IQR = 8, Team B has IQR = 22. What does this tell you?
choices: Team A's middle 50% is more consistent; Team B's is more spread out
Team B is a better team
Team A has a higher median
The IQRs don't tell you about consistency
core.explanation: A smaller IQR means the middle 50% of data is more tightly clustered. Team A's scoring is more consistent in the middle range.
feedback: Bigger IQR doesn't mean better—it means more variation.
IQR tells consistency—smaller is tighter.
IQR is always about consistency in the middle 50%.
hints: IQR measures the width of the box — how spread out the MIDDLE 50% of each team's scores is.
Compare a narrow box (IQR 8) with a wide box (IQR 22). Ask what narrow vs wide says about consistency — not about which team is better.
First step: translate each number — Team A's middle scores span only 8 points; Team B's span 22. Then choose the statement that matches.

core.explanation: Q1 is the MEDIAN of the lower half, not just one of its values. The lower half is 4, 8, 10, 14 — an even-sized group — so Q1 = (8 + 10) ÷ 2 = 9, not 10. The student grabbed a single value instead of averaging the two middle numbers of the half.
hints: When a half has an even number of values, the quartile is the average of its two middle values.
Lower half 4, 8, 10, 14: the two middle values are 8 and 10, so Q1 = (8 + 10) ÷ 2 = 9.

stretch.prompt: A basketball player scored 15, 18, 16, 42, and 14 points in 5 games. Find the mean and median. Which better represents the player's typical game? Explain how the outlier affects each measure.
stretch.frame: Mean = ___. Median = ___. The ___ better represents a typical game because the outlier (___) pulls the ___ toward it, making it ___ than most scores. The median is not affected because ___.
stretch.explanation: The five scores add to 105, so the mean is 105 ÷ 5 = 21, while the ordered list 14, 15, 16, 18, 42 gives a median of 16. The 42-point game is an outlier that drags the mean up above four of the five games, but the median only cares about position, so 16 better represents a typical game.
hints: One game (42 points) is far above the others — that's your outlier. Keep it in mind as you find both measures.
Plan: (1) mean = sum of the 5 scores ÷ 5, (2) median = middle of the ordered scores, (3) decide which lands closer to most games.
Step 1: add 15 + 18 + 16 + 42 + 14 and divide by 5. Then order the scores least to greatest and circle the 3rd — compare the two results.

stretch.explanation: Q1 is the median of the lower half (3, 7, 9), which is 7. Q3 is the median of the upper half (15, 18, 21), which is 18. The student used the wrong value for Q1 — they picked 9 (the last value in the lower half) instead of the median of that half.
hints: Q1 is not just a value in the lower half — it is the MEDIAN of the lower half.
Lower half: 3, 7, 9. The median of these three values is 7, not 9.

stretch.prompt: Two basketball teams played 9 games each. Team A: 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 52, 54, 56. Team B: 30, 35, 40, 45, 48, 50, 55, 60, 65. Find the five-number summary and IQR for each team. Which team is more consistent? Which has a wider spread in the middle 50%?
stretch.frame: Team A: Min=___, Q1=___, Median=___, Q3=___, Max=___, IQR=___. Team B: Min=___, Q1=___, Median=___, Q3=___, Max=___, IQR=___. Team ___ is more consistent because its IQR is ___.
stretch.explanation: Team A's summary is 40, 43, 48, 53, 56 with IQR = 53 − 43 = 10, and Team B's is 30, 37.5, 48, 57.5, 65 with IQR = 57.5 − 37.5 = 20. Both teams share a median of 48, but Team B's middle 50% spreads twice as far, so Team A is the more consistent team.
hints: Both score lists are already ordered, 9 games each — so the 5th score is each team's median. That's your anchor point.
For each team: Min = 1st value, Max = 9th, Median = 5th. Q1 = middle of the first four, Q3 = middle of the last four. Then IQR = Q3 − Q1.
Team A first: Min = 40, Max = 56, Median = 48 (the 5th value). Now average 42 and 44 for Q1, and 52 and 54 for Q3.
